opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually really validating to see Google put out Gemini Diffusion. For a long time, when we were talking about diffusion for language, a lot of people were skeptical. The conventional wisdom was that autoregressive models had won, that text is inherently sequential, and that diffusion was something that worked for images and video but not for discrete data like language and code. So when a lab like Google DeepMind invests in this direction and shows strong results, it sends a clear signal to the whole field that this is a serious alternative, not just an academic curiosity.

In terms of positioning, Google obviously has enormous advantages. They have compute, they have data, they have incredible researchers, and they have distribution through all their products. I don't want to downplay any of that. But I think a focused company like ours has some real advantages too. For us, diffusion language models aren't one bet among many; this is the whole company. Everything we do, from the research to the inference stack to the serving infrastructure, is built around making diffusion models work really well in production. That focus matters, because getting these models to be fast and reliable at scale requires a lot of new engineering. You can't just take the existing autoregressive serving infrastructure and drop a diffusion model into it. The kernels, the batching strategies, the way you think about latency and throughput, all of that changes.

There's also a speed of execution question. In a large organization, even when the research is excellent, bringing something to production means navigating a lot of competing priorities. Their flagship models are autoregressive, and that's where most of their product investment goes. For us, we've been able to put models in the hands of developers and enterprise customers, learn from real use cases like code completion and editing, latency-sensitive applications, and agentic workflows, and iterate very quickly.

And honestly, I think the market is big enough that having multiple players pushing diffusion forward is good for everyone. It grows the ecosystem, it gets more people building tooling and thinking about how to use these models, and it helps educate customers that there's a different trade-off curve available, where you can get much higher throughput and lower latency at comparable quality. So I see Google more as a validation of the thesis than as a threat. Our job is to keep being the ones who push the frontier of what these models can do and make them the easiest to deploy in practice.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so first of all, I think it's great that Google is doing this. When we started Inception, diffusion for language was still kind of a fringe idea, and a lot of people were skeptical that it could work at all for text. So having a company like Google come out with Gemini Diffusion and show that, yes, you can get very high quality and very high throughput with a diffusion-based language model, that's a huge validation for the whole approach. It basically settles the question of whether this is a real direction, and it's good for us because it means we spend less time convincing people that the paradigm makes sense.

In terms of their position, obviously Google has enormous advantages. They have the compute, they have the data, they have the TPU stack, and they have distribution through all their products. If they decide to push hard on this, they can do a lot. But I also think it's worth noting that for them, diffusion is one of many bets. They have the main Gemini line, which is autoregressive, and there's a big organizational and infrastructure investment behind that. Everything from serving to tooling to how they do post-training is built around that paradigm. So shifting a large part of their production stack over to a fundamentally different way of generating text is not a small thing, even for Google. There's a lot of inertia.

For us, this is the only thing we do. We're not hedging. All of our research, our engineering, our serving infrastructure, everything is built from the ground up around diffusion. And a lot of the hard work in making these models practical is not just in the modeling, it's in the systems side. How you actually exploit the parallelism at inference time, how you handle variable length generation, how you do things like tool use and structured outputs, how you make it work on existing GPU hardware rather than custom silicon. Those are problems where being focused and moving fast really matters, and where I think a small team can actually be ahead.

The other thing I'd say is that the market for this is really large. There's a huge amount of demand for fast, cheap inference, especially in things like coding, agents, and any application where latency matters a lot. So I don't really see this as a zero-sum thing where Google wins or we win. I think the pie is big enough, and frankly, I think a few years from now a lot of language models will be using some form of parallel generation. The question is who gets there first with something developers actually want to use, and I feel pretty good about where we are.

astra-6.text:
Google has some clear advantages: enormous resources, strong research teams, and the infrastructure to bring a model to a lot of users. But getting a model into production also means making choices about the product, the latency, the cost, and how it fits into existing systems. Resources alone don’t settle all of those questions.

For a focused startup like ours, the advantage is that this is our central priority. We can move quickly, make decisions around the technology, and work closely with customers to understand where it’s useful. The challenge is that we have to be selective about where we invest.

So I wouldn’t frame it as one side having every advantage. Google is very well positioned, and a startup has room to compete through focus and execution.

sol-6.1.text:
Google has tremendous resources, both in terms of research talent and the infrastructure to bring something like Gemini Diffusion to users. So I would take them very seriously. At the same time, there’s a difference between demonstrating a compelling model and building a product around it. A focused startup can move quickly, make this its central priority, and work closely with customers to figure out where the technology is most useful.

I don’t think the outcome is predetermined. The question is how well you translate the advantages of diffusion into something people actually want to use. Speed matters, but so do quality, reliability, and how the model fits into someone’s workflow.
